The current educational landscape is characterized by diverse multimedia content such as videos, images, and text. Despite the growing interest in leveraging machine learning for educational purposes, most existing models have limitations when dealing with complex multimodal educational materials. This is largely due to the lack of effective methods for multimodal fusion. To address this challenge, we propose a novel multimodal fusion method that utilizes a graph attention network to learn representations from multiple educational modalities. Our approach is grounded in the assumption that different modalities within a multimedia educational content set form a complex network structure. In this network, nodes represent individual modalities while edges indicate relationships between them. We employ a graph attention network to learn representations by attending to the relationships between modalities. Our approach is evaluated using a large-scale dataset of educational videos, and the results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art models. Additionally, our model achieves high generalization performance when applied to novel educational domains, and the code is made publicly available. For more information, please visit our project website at https://github.com/zhengdongguo/Multimodal-Graph-Attention-Network. For educational purposes, our model is integrated with an interactive platform at https://ai4ed.xu.edu.cn/mgan. We also provide a demo video at https://youtu.be/8Gk0J6N6TgQ. Our research contribution is threefold: (1) a novel multimodal fusion method that utilizes a graph attention network to learn educational representations; (2) a large-scale dataset of educational videos for evaluating multimodal fusion methods; (3) a platform for interactive AI-assisted learning. Our research has the potential to be applied in various domains, including education, multimedia processing, and natural language processing. Our study is grounded in a substantial dataset comprising over 1.2 million text sequences extracted from a large-scale botnet operation, which lasted several months. The D{0} collaboration recalibrated the Jet Energy Corrections in their analysis of the top quark mass using data from the CDF experiment. This study presents the details of the D{0} investigation into the JEC recalibration and discusses the implications for the world's top quark mass average. We introduce DART, a distributed algorithm designed to solve multi-agent reinforcement learning challenges through decentralized learning. DART aims to maximize the overall reward by synchronizing local Q-function approximations among agents despite communication constraints. A key aspect of DART is its ability to achieve faster convergence than existing methods, even in complex environments. Our theoretical analysis and empirical studies reveal that DART surpasses previous algorithms in solving the mean reward maximization problem and approaches the optimal rate of convergence in centralized settings. Furthermore, DART demonstrates the capacity to solve a broader range of problems, including tasks that utilize count-sketch data structures to accommodate communication-limited scenarios. Additionally, DART exhibits improved performance in multi-agent cooperative Q-learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning tasks, as observed in our experimental results. These findings validate the potential of DART as a powerful tool for addressing multi-agent reinforcement learning challenges through decentralized learning. This study introduces a novel approach to utilizing fact descriptions in summarization, 
which leverages rich contextual information to refine the summarization process. 
Although fact descriptions offer valuable context, their integration in fact-based summarization 
remains underexplored due to the absence of a standard training framework. 
To address this gap, we propose a new architecture that combines the strengths of both 
fact-based and abstraction-based summarization techniques. 
Our model, which can be trained using existing datasets, employs a novel training strategy 
to incorporate fact descriptions and achieve two key benefits: richer summary content and 
reliable fact verification capabilities. 
Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our model, yielding more 
informative summaries and achieving state-of-the-art fact verification accuracy. 
Furthermore, our model's abstractive capabilities are validated through human evaluation, 
which highlights its ability to generate coherent summaries that accurately reflect fact descriptions. 
The model's code and models are made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yanicul/fact-descriptions-sum. 
Our findings indicate promising prospects for fact-based summarization and open up new avenues 
for exploration. The accompanying data and code can be found at https://github.com/yanicul/fact-descriptions-sum.

The study of superheavy nuclei's competition between alpha decay and beta plus (β+)/electron capture has been investigated using theoretical calculations. However, when only a few expert demonstrations are available, it's challenging to strike the right balance between overfitting and underfitting. To tackle this issue, we present a new approach called SoftDICE, which employs a Bayesian framework to generate a soft Dirichlet distribution over proposed actions. This distribution is then used to calculate a confidence measure for each action-observation pair, allowing for more efficient use of limited demonstrations. By doing so, SoftDICE achieves superior sample efficiency by effectively balancing expert trajectories and preventing underfitting in the policy. Experimental results on continuous control tasks demonstrate the superiority of SoftDICE over existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its ability to generate more diverse and effective trajectories. Additionally, the confidence measure in SoftDICE can be used to identify and rectify IRL algorithm failures, such as dataset biases and adversarial samples. The purpose of this research is to develop a method to assess the effectiveness of low-pass and high-pass filters used in image processing and filtering. However, the quality of these filters is subjective and depends on various criteria. This study proposes a quantitative method to evaluate low-pass and high-pass filters by assessing their ability to preserve or remove image features. To achieve this, the study utilizes a deep network trained on natural images, which is used to segment the images into their areas of interest and non-interest. Subsequently, the performance of the low-pass and high-pass filters is evaluated by comparing their output against the non-interest regions and areas of interest respectively. This method is applied to various filters, including a Gaussian filter, wavelet filters, and a U-Net, to demonstrate its effectiveness. Moreover, the study highlights the potential applications of this approach in image processing, including denoising, deblurring, deblocking, and compression. This method can also be used to evaluate the effectiveness of filters in reducing artifacts in images that have been subject to various types of disturbances. This metric is used to assess the effectiveness of various deblocking filters, which are then compared to their performance in the denoising and deblurring tasks. Finally, the study also investigates the effectiveness of compression algorithms on images that have been filtered to reduce noise and restore their visual quality. The proposed methods are implemented in the C++ programming language and are available for download on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/abdullah-ahmad/Filter-Evaluation. The reliability of group differences in brain network changes can be compromised by inter-site effects in functional connectivity measurements. To address this issue, we developed an analytical framework for detecting group differences in brain networks that incorporates various confounding factors, including those related to different measurement sites. Our method, known as CATE-FC, utilizes a mixed-effects model to account for both site-specific and individual variations in functional connectivity matrices. Through simulations, we demonstrated that CATE-FC outperforms traditional network analysis techniques in identifying individual differences and group differences, especially when dealing with multiple confounding sites. Our analysis of resting-state functional connectivity data from the Human Connectome Project also revealed that CATE-FC provides more accurate results than conventional methods in the presence of multiple measurement sites. Furthermore, CATE-FC offers the flexibility to incorporate site-specific factors and can be used to investigate the relationship between site-specific factors and individual differences in functional connectivity. Our results suggest that CATE-FC is a valuable tool for analyzing functional connectivity data that may vary across multiple measurement sites. To address this, researchers have developed various methods for enhancing the robustness of CNNs and evaluated their performance using metrics like accuracy and Jacobian norms. However, these metrics have their limitations, as they focus solely on the network's output sensitivity to small variations without considering its overall performance across a range of perturbations. We also propose an innovative training approach that utilizes the Robustness Ratio to guide the learning process. This paper examines the stability of multi-agent systems through a Lyapunov stability perspective and introduces the concept of mean-field interacting systems, where individual agents are influenced by the overall ensemble average. Our theoretical framework for interacting mean-field dynamical systems, or MF-IDS, encompasses a broader scope of multi-agent systems, and we develop necessary conditions for stability using Lyapunov's first theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach to a broader class of nonlinear systems by deriving a linearized stability criterion. To validate our theory, we develop two novel distributed tracking control strategies for multi-agent systems, and extensive numerical simulations illustrate the effectiveness of our method in handling large-scale networks. Additional simulations also confirm the accuracy of our linearized stability condition. Our research also reveals the significant impact of interconnection among agents on system stability, and we demonstrate the feasibility of our method in controlling multi-agent systems with significant nonlinearities. Ultimately, our work provides a foundational framework for analyzing the stability of multi-agent systems, and we demonstrate the potential for our method to be applied in real-world scenarios like autonomous vehicle tracking. Recent breakthroughs in zero-shot learning have been achieved by recent large-scale pre-trained vision-lingua models, particularly CLIP. Nonetheless, its performance is hindered by the scarcity of high-quality human-annotated data. To address this issue, we introduce Domain Prompt Learning (DPL), a novel approach that enables zero-shot learning without additional human annotation costs. By leveraging a domain discriminator and domain conditional alignment, DPL generates domain-specific prompts, thereby improving the model's domain adaptability. Experimentation demonstrates that DPL can effectively enhance the model's performance on unseen datasets, even when the model has been initially pre-trained on a range of general-purpose image datasets. Notably, DPL achieves a remarkable accuracy of 48.1% on the ImageNet dataset, surpassing the baseline by 2.1%. A novel approach to evaluating reduced-reference dehazed image quality estimates the degree of perceived dehazing based on original and dehazed image differences. This method leverages the fact that dehazing methods alter both the dehazed image and its differences. As a result, using reduced-reference information in conjunction with image differences enables the capture of dehazing artifacts affecting the dehazed image. Subsequently, dehazed image quality is assessed by quantifying the correlation between predicted scores and the perceived dehazed image quality, obtained through subjective evaluations. This approach yields a novel metric for evaluating dehazed image quality in reduced-reference settings, outperforming existing metrics in this domain, according to experimental results on two public datasets. Notably, the proposed metric requires minimal additional data, as it utilizes image differences from the original and dehazed images rather than supplementary features. This approach is further enhanced by employing a deep learning-based framework to optimize the metric for dehazed image quality evaluation. Ultimately, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art reduced-reference dehazed image quality evaluation techniques. Deep survival models have become increasingly popular for predicting patient survival in fields like medicine and biology, where understanding why a model makes predictions is just as important as the predictions themselves. Current explainability methods for deep survival models often rely on approximations, which can lead to a disconnect between predicted outcomes and the underlying reasons for them. In response, we introduce a new explainability framework for deep survival models, called the Reverse Survival Model (RSM). By reversing the process of typical deep survival models, RSM generates explanations that are tailored to specific predictions and are more accurate, efficient, and transparent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RSM in improving the explainability of predictions made by a well-known deep survival model, and our approach is validated through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Furthermore, we show that RSM can be adapted to other tasks, such as counterfactual explanations and causal analysis, which can help address more complex problems in deep survival models. Our work is accompanied by a comprehensive implementation on GitHub, which includes code and scripts for reproducing our results. This research has significant implications for the development of more transparent and interpretable deep survival models for applications in healthcare and beyond. This research introduces a novel, unified control approach for legged robots with multi-fingered hands that integrate predictive control and trajectory planning. The proposed method optimizes trajectory timing to maintain balance and manipulate objects, while simultaneously planning precise movements for the robot's joints and gripper fingers. The integration of predictive control enables the development of a comprehensive, low-level control strategy that leverages predictive models to mitigate external disturbances. The unified control approach was successfully tested on a quadruped robot with a gripper-equipped hand, demonstrating its effectiveness in tasks such as picking up objects, navigating through tight spaces, and manipulating objects while moving. Experimental results validate the proposed method's superiority in its ability to balance and regulate interaction forces. The developed control approach is versatile and can be applied to various robotic platforms, including those with multi-fingered hands. Furthermore, this work can serve as a foundation for future research on control strategies for robots that can perform multiple tasks concurrently. In positive and unlabeled learning, systems generate labeled data, but only provide positive instances with a label, leaving the negative instances without labels. Existing methods for positive and unlabeled learning often rely on a two-step approach, using pseudo-labeling to create some labeled negative instances and then adjusting the model's parameters to minimize errors. However, these methods have limitations due to their reliance on a two-step approach and the assumption that pseudo-labels are accurate. To address this issue, we introduce a single-step framework called ImPULSeS, which uses the model's predictive distribution to determine the likelihood of unlabeled instances being negative and then adjusts the model's parameters based on the predicted negative instances. This allows ImPULSeS to be more robust and accurate, especially in the presence of class imbalance. Experimental results show that ImPULSeS outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in positive and unlabeled learning. Additionally, ImPULSeS is shown to be more efficient than existing frameworks, requiring fewer training instances to achieve the same level of accuracy. The acquisition of certain imaging techniques can be made more efficient by interweaving data across multiple scan lines. This efficiency gain is due to the fact that each scan line relies on its corresponding neighbors, both above and below, during reconstruction. However, this efficiency comes at the expense of slower scan times, which can lead to data loss due to mechanical movement. This paper introduces a new approach to mitigate these data losses by drawing from the field of compressed sensing. By applying a novel optimization method that leverages the sparsity of data across interwoven scan lines, data can now be reconstructed from partially acquired scans. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulated and real-world experiments. Additionally, this research explores the benefits of employing multiple optimization strategies in conjunction with each other. These strategies are then applied to a custom-built MRI scanner. Experiments have shown that the method's performance is comparable to traditional methods under various sampling conditions, while also exhibiting robustness in the presence of random data variations. These findings hold significant implications for future MRI acquisition strategies that rely on interwoven scan lines. In conventional C-RAN systems, data from each user is transmitted to the data fusion center via fronthaul, which can become a bottleneck due to limited capacity. A new, split-up approach transmits only relevant data from the BS to the DC, reducing transmission rates. Two DC precoder designs have been developed to minimize this transmission rate. The first design uses a power-splitting approach, splitting data between multiple precoded copies of the same information, with each copy having a predetermined power level. The second approach, utilizing superposition coding, allows multiple data streams to be transmitted together. Wink is a secure system that allows users to store encrypted messages, revealing only the encrypted form, not the original content. Furthermore, Wink's benefits are demonstrated in the context of a real-world scenario involving a Ukrainian refugee who successfully stored her 2048-bit encryption keys and accessed vital services, like Ukrainian voter registration, despite the risks associated with her coerced situation. We analyze a class of quantum analogs to Seiberg-Witten curves that exhibit spontaneous PT-symmetry breaking as realized in complex elliptic curves with non-trivial holomorphic maps onto the complex plane. This family of curves is characterized by their use in modeling low-energy Hamiltonians associated with two-dimensional topological systems hosting gapless edge modes protected by parity and time reversal symmetries. To investigate the underlying physics, we employ a computational approach to generate discrete approximations of these PT-symmetric curves and subsequently analyze their properties in terms of the parity-time reversal matrix's spectral properties. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of the curve's Bergman point as a function of the curve's parameter space and demonstrate the existence of a new metric for defining Bergman points in complex elliptic curves. This research also explores the relationship between the curve's parameter space, the curve's geometry, and the resulting low-energy Hamiltonians. To validate our findings, we numerically solve the time-dependent Schrodinger equation for the resulting systems and verify that the obtained wave functions exhibit the expected parity and time reversal symmetry properties. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the low-energy physics governed by the Seiberg-Witten curves and highlights the utility of these curves in the study of topological systems hosting gapless edge modes. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these findings in the study of topological systems within higher-dimensional spaces. This research also explores the potential connections between the Seiberg-Witten curves and the recently proposed concept of quantum exceptional points. This research introduces the Multi Point-Voxel Convolution (MPVConv) model, a novel point cloud processing framework that surpasses the performance of existing point-based and voxel-based models. MPVConv utilizes a voxel-based approach, with a unique multi-point convolutional mechanism that enables the efficient aggregation of local point relationships within voxels. By employing a kernel-based method to calculate voxel entries, MPVConv can effectively represent the spatial point distribution within a voxel. This results in a more accurate and informative representation compared to traditional one-point convolution models like PointNet and their voxel-based counterparts. Furthermore, MPVConv outperforms voxel-based models like Point Convolution (PCN++) in the N-Primitives dataset, with competitive accuracy and significantly reduced memory requirements. Additionally, a variant of MPVConv, MPVConv++, is proposed, which leverages a graph-based approach to refine voxel representations through local point connections. Experimental results demonstrate that MPVConv and its variants outperform existing models in 3D object detection tasks, with MPVConv++ achieving superior performance with only 0.6% extra memory. To mitigate power imbalances on the transmission network, High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) interconnects neighboring areas, allowing for flexible flow reversal. We investigate the potential benefits of HVDC flow reversal for hydro-encircled countries in relation to their energy security. A novel, practical method is developed to determine the FRR capacity of an HVDC link, dependent on hydroelectric generation. A two-stage optimization model is then used to optimize power system operation, with the first stage determining HVDC power reversals and the second stage optimizing hydroelectric generation and non-hydroelectric unit commitment. A case study on the Nordic countries' future power system, with the potential introduction of HVDC reversals, reveals that a significant FRR capacity of 3.5 GW is achievable. This, in turn, reduces the Nordic countries' electricity imports by 1.7 TWh and lowers CO2 emissions by 1.3 Mt, assuming a high share of renewable energy in the electricity mix. However, the total system costs decrease only slightly, indicating that HVDC reversals are more effective in enhancing energy security than in reducing costs. This outcome suggests that energy security benefits from HVDC reversals primarily stem from hydroelectric power plants, which can provide the necessary flexibility and energy security resilience. A sensitivity analysis on hydroelectric capacity, electricity demand, and HVDC capacity confirms the robustness of these results. Additionally, the study reveals that a hydroelectric capacity of 2 GW can provide energy security benefits equivalent to an HVDC capacity of 1.5 GW, under the same assumptions. This highlights the importance of hydroelectric power plants in providing energy security resilience and highlights the need for hydroelectric expansion in the Nordic countries. Finally, the study's results demonstrate that a well-designed HVDC system, with sufficient HVDC capacity and flexibility, can enhance energy security resilience in the Nordic countries. This, in turn, reduces the need for additional cross-border interconnectors and increases the Nordic countries' ability to withstand power imbalances, particularly during extreme scenarios. However, the study's findings also indicate that a highly flexible Nordic energy system, with HVDC reversals, is still vulnerable to power imbalances, particularly in extreme scenarios. This vulnerability necessitates the development of additional resilience measures to ensure the Nordic countries' energy security. This, in turn, highlights the need for further research on developing effective resilience measures to address the vulnerabilities in the Nordic energy system. Our analysis explores the historical development of resource theories, which have emerged as a valuable tool in both theoretical and applied physics contexts. By examining the current state of resource theory frameworks, we identify a set of fundamental questions that arise when applying these theories to real-world physical systems. Through a detailed examination of the quantum theory of measurement, we demonstrate how resource theories can serve as a bridge between physical theories and their practical implementations, thereby shedding light on the underlying operational principles. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges associated with developing a resource theory for quantum gravity, which may ultimately require the creation of novel mathematical structures that transcend the existing frameworks of quantum mechanics and general relativity. By leveraging this insight, we can gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental nature of the physical systems in question. We introduce the DDF inspector-executor framework, which accelerates sparse matrix multiplication and the solution of sparse triangular systems by breaking down input and output matrices into smaller sub-matrices. This framework is integrated into the SciDS library, a component of the DDF library, to enhance sparse direct solvers. Two key features are presented: first, a solver-independent optimization strategy for matrix factorization and solving; second, an efficient tiling of the factorization process to minimize memory usage during the same program run. Experimental results demonstrate significant performance improvements for various sparse direct solvers on numerous test cases, achieving up to 4.9x speedup compared to their unoptimized versions within the same library. These improvements are largely due to the efficient use of memory, resulting in a reduced average memory usage of 0.7% to 1.4% of the total input matrix. Effective collaboration with AI teammates is crucial for achieving human-AI teamwork goals, yet understanding how team dynamics and AI interactions impact communication quality remains limited. This study investigates communication patterns in AI teams within the DiDi framework, focusing on the influence of team members' impressions of each other on collaboration. We collected data from 1,542 DiDi teams and found that positive team impressions and strong communication early in the game, particularly from lead to non-lead roles, significantly improved overall communication quality. However, when evaluating the impact of AI teammates on human players, we found that this dependence was reversed, highlighting the need for AI teammates to be perceptive of human teammates' strengths to foster a supportive partnership. The study's findings also suggest that AI teammates should be designed to provide constructive, task-focused feedback rather than positive affirmations. The study's results provide valuable insights for enhancing human-AI collaboration and the development of more effective AI teammates. The data collected during this study is publicly available on the Human-AI Collaboration Dataset repository. Furthermore, we propose the development of a new game, DiDi, to facilitate the exploration of AI teammate design, and offer suggestions for future research in the field. A novel approach to proof, known as proof-by-simulation, leverages the capabilities of programmable verifiers to establish bounds on a program's properties, which can then be extended to the analysis of complex systems. In this study, we demonstrate the utility of proof-by-simulation in determining the operating characteristics of statistical designs. We achieve this by developing a framework that enables the computation of approximate distributions for key metrics, such as sample means, using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Moreover, our research shows that these distributions can be approximated through the solution of stochastic differential equations, which can be efficiently solved using probabilistic programming languages. The results of our study indicate that our approach can produce accurate distributions for large datasets, thereby offering a valuable solution for researchers seeking to understand the implications of sampling in statistical contexts. The findings of this work also highlight the potential for future research in the application of proof-by-simulation to the analysis of complex statistical systems. Wasserstein distance-based clustering methods have shown potential in handling clustered distributions with multimodal heavy-tailed characteristics. Our study focuses on evaluating the performance of the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm, particularly on synthetic data generated from heavy-tailed distributions, as well as real-world datasets such as images and text. We conducted a comparative analysis with traditional clustering algorithms, observing that Wasserstein $k$-means outperformed its competitors in handling data with high levels of contamination and multimodal patterns using the Sum of Squared Distances metric. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that Wasserstein $k$-means is resilient to outliers and data irregularities, making it a suitable choice for clustering tasks. However, our study also uncovered instances where Wasserstein $k$-means struggled to accurately segment data with highly dissimilar cluster sizes and significantly underperformed when recovering clusters with vastly different mean values. To address these limitations, we proposed a novel approach to handle unequal cluster sizes by introducing a bias term into the objective function of the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm. Our findings demonstrate that this method effectively handles unequal cluster sizes and outperforms traditional clustering methods across various synthetic and real-world datasets. Additionally, our analysis revealed that incorporating a bias term into the objective function of the Wasserstein $k$-means algorithm is essential for accurately recovering clusters with vastly different mean values. Our study contributes to the development of robust and effective clustering methods for handling high-dimensional data with multimodal heavy-tailed characteristics. Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the development of neural networks capable of generating complex and detailed explanations for their predictions, particularly in fault diagnosis.  However, the creation of detailed explanations in the form of natural language requires significant computational resources and often results in overly elaborate justifications.  In contrast, our proposed approach, Guided Neural Networks, incorporates a structural component to its architecture, enabling it to generate clear and concise explanations in the form of formal language.  By doing so, our approach addresses the common issue of over-explanation inherent in neural networks.  Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed GNNs not only achieve superior fault diagnosis performance but also produce more effective and concise explanations compared to existing state-of-the-art models.  Moreover, the structured explanations generated by our approach are amenable to further analysis using formal methods, thereby enhancing their interpretability and modularity.  Our implementation of the GNNs is openly accessible on GitHub, providing researchers with a means to experiment and build upon our findings.  An accompanying case study illustrates the practical application of our approach in identifying design errors in a critical system.  Our research indicates that the proposed GNNs have the potential to serve as a versatile and efficient tool for a wide range of fault diagnosis tasks. Quantum circuits can be efficiently modeled by sampling from classical distributions that closely resemble the output of the circuit, a technique known as recompilation. This method allows for the simulation of complex circuits with limited quantum resources, and its effectiveness can be quantified by measuring average mutual information. A straightforward recompilation method is presented, and it is shown that certain components of the recompilation process can be optimized through the use of deep neural networks. By employing such networks to optimize circuit components, including rotation gates and entangling gates, and by comparing their performance to an optimal baseline, it is found that optimization can significantly enhance the effectiveness of the recompilation process. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the optimal parameters of the neural networks can be discovered through the use of a gradient-based optimization algorithm, and it is shown that this approach can be effectively used to simulate complex quantum circuits with high accuracy. Finally, it is found that the optimal parameters of the neural networks can be effectively compressed into a single set of parameters, and that this approach can be used to generate highly accurate quantum circuits that can be easily scaled up for the simulation of complex quantum systems. This approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of quantum simulation by enabling the simulation of complex quantum circuits with high accuracy and without the need for large-scale quantum hardware. To address these issues, we propose a new framework that leverages vehicles' real-time data to enhance federated learning. By integrating vehicles into aggregation and training processes, we significantly improve model accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations involving multiple vehicles, showcasing its benefits in terms of accuracy and training time. The results show that our method achieves higher model accuracy compared to conventional edge federated learning methods. By focusing on local image regions, the method effectively resolves the ambiguity inherent in image-based face reconstruction. To achieve optimal results, the approach is carefully optimized to balance global and local image consistency. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed model's ability to produce highly accurate 3D face models from a single image, outperforming existing methods in terms of quality and accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is extended to enable the generation of 3D face models from a single video, utilizing optical flow estimation to address the challenges of non-rigid motion and subject occlusion. Our study also shows that when developers remove feature toggles, they tend to be associated with more branch merges and push commits compared to when they add them. These results offer initial insights into the impact of feature toggles on software development and maintenance. Our study indicates that while feature toggles can be an effective solution for temporary issues, they may have negative consequences for software projects, particularly smaller ones. Therefore, further research is needed to identify more lasting solutions for addressing similar problems. We introduce a novel self-supervised approach to learning that employs denoising,
enabling the development of robust models capable of generalizing their knowledge
across various data sources. In this framework, a denoiser is trained to restore
corrupted images using only a single noisy image as a reference. This is achieved
by creating pairs of clean and corrupted images through different types of noise
distortion and training a model to denoise between them. Our experiments demonstrate
that this method consistently improves performance in downstream tasks, such as
image denoising and image classification, regardless of the dataset used. This
flexibility is achieved by learning a universal denoising solution that can be
applied to diverse datasets. Furthermore, we show that the denoising process
enhances the disentanglement of image features, leading to improved generalization
capabilities. To support further research, we provide a dedicated codebase and
release a new dataset of images with diverse types of noise for training and
testing denoising models. Our code and dataset can be found at
https://github.com/ComputerVisionGroup/denosing-self-supervised-learning. 
Additionally, we have developed a new dataset called "Worst Case Scenarios" 
containing images with challenging noise types that are difficult to remove. 
This dataset can be found at https://github.com/ComputerVisionGroup/worst-case-scenarios. 
The datasets used in our research can be found at https://github.com/ComputerVisionClever. 
Our research is also discussed in our blog post at 
https://www.computer-vision.net/denosing-self-supervised-learning.

Experimental results demonstrate the superior quality of the converted voices produced by our model, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both subjective and objective evaluation metrics. This study delves into the phenomenon of emotion contagion through the lens of influence diffusion. Emotion contagion occurs when individuals mimic the emotions of others through exposure to their content, which can be either positive or negative in sentiment. Building on existing research, we develop a probabilistic model to describe the process of emotional contagion through social influence. Our model, which accounts for individual differences in susceptibility to social influence, predicts that consuming content with negative sentiment has a greater impact on emotion contagion than consuming content with positive sentiment. Additionally, we find that the likelihood of emotion contagion depends not only on individual susceptibility but also on the content's emotional value. To validate our theoretical findings, we employ a two-stage model on Twitter data and provide empirical evidence to support our predictions. Our results indicate that the emotional contagion model is a reliable tool for understanding the diffusion of emotions in online social networks and can be a valuable asset in managing online social influence for practitioners. Ultimately, we envision that our work will contribute significantly to the development of effective methods for managing online social influence and mitigating the harmful effects of emotion contagion on individuals and society. This paper explores the concept of free Fuss-Catalan sequences over a cyclic group, as well as the properties of natural number sequences associated with the group, drawing inspiration from earlier work on the free Catalan sequence and natural number sequence. We identify key relationships between these sequences and establish a connection between the natural number sequences and the exponential generating function for Fuss-Catalan numbers, ultimately providing explicit formulae for the sequences and their generalizations. This work also examines the properties of the free Fuss-Catalan sequence and its underlying combinatorial structure. Additionally, we show that this method can be utilized as a reward function in conventional reinforcement learning techniques. The increasing use of facial recognition technology in modern applications has raised concerns over its security, particularly in the face of malicious backdoor attacks.  Existing defense methods are often ineffective as they either don't provide sufficient protection or become vulnerable to more sophisticated attacks.  In response, we have developed a novel approach called BA-BAM that leverages knowledge distillation to improve the resilience of face recognition models against a range of sophisticated backdoor threats.  BA-BAM successfully defends against both clean and noisy backdoor attacks by combining two key elements: a novel distillation loss function that is robust to clean backdoor triggers and a feature-based loss function that targets noisy triggers.  Through this approach, BA-BAM can dynamically adapt to different types of backdoor threats through a simple adjustment of its clean trigger shape, without requiring additional model training.  In addition, our approach is flexible and can be easily integrated into existing face recognition models.  Our experiments demonstrate BA-BAM's effectiveness in significantly improving the robustness of face recognition models against a range of sophisticated backdoor threats, including those that are resistant to traditional defense methods.  For example, our approach can reduce the attack success rate by 60.2% on a heavily compromised model that was originally 100% effective against a clean model. This unentangling does not affect the classical Hamiltonian's relationship with the quantum Hamiltonian. This study presents a novel, adaptable approach for distinguishing between pulsation signals and transit events in light curves. The method leverages the Fourier domain by applying a two-stage process. In the initial stage, it utilizes the Morlet Wavelet transform to break down light curves into contiguous segments, and subsequently isolates the signal components from noise to generate a set of "signal-only" light curves. These are then used to estimate the signal's power spectrum in each segment. In the subsequent stage, it employs a weighted least-squares method to fit the power spectrum with a specific model, and then utilizes this model to predict the signal's behavior in the Fourier domain. Predicted signals are subtracted from the original data, yielding a new set of light curves that are predominantly devoid of pulsation signals. In contrast, the remaining data is likely to contain transit events, which can be isolated and analyzed to derive the transit parameters. This approach was successfully tested on synthetic light curves and demonstrated to be effective in separating pulsation signals from transit events. Furthermore, the approach was applied to real light curves of stars with varying degrees of pulsation signals and transit events, yielding promising results. As each secondary leader's messages are validated, the most recent messages are incorporated into the graph and considered as historical data, ensuring the secure and efficient operation of the protocol. We suggest an innovative method for approximating the shortest path distance between nodes in massive networks by leveraging advancements in deep learning. Our approach employs vector embeddings of nodes to estimate distances, and we develop an efficient algorithm that iteratively updates these estimates for all nodes in the network. Empirical testing of real-world networks confirms that our method converges rapidly to accurate distances. Notably, this algorithm's speed is linearly proportional to the number of nodes, making it suitable for handling extremely large networks where traditional methods prove impractical. Our approach also enables the development of a data structure that accelerates the detection of triangles in massive graphs by a linear factor. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our method in approximating network distances for various other tasks, including clustering and community detection. Our results indicate that these techniques achieve the same quality of outcomes as their exact counterparts while executing tasks significantly faster. This advantage can result in speedup factors of up to 1.6 for community detection and 1.1 for triangle counting at the cost of a minimal 2% increase in running time. This research introduces a novel approach to reducing the computational demands of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), focusing on the computation-intensive convolutional layers. Our proposed solution combines pruning and quantization to minimize the impact of these layers on overall inference times. First, we utilize pruning to decrease the number of parameters, followed by the application of quantization to convert remaining parameters to low-bit integer values. This allows for the utilization of highly optimized CPU-based integer multiplication and accumulation instructions, significantly accelerating the inference process. We evaluate the effectiveness of our pruning strategy, an L1-based method, on various CNN architectures and datasets, demonstrating its ability to achieve high compression ratios with minimal accuracy degradation. Our pruning results show that, for a given CNN, the number of parameters can be reduced by 50% to achieve a minimal performance loss of 1% accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our pruning approach, in conjunction with quantization, enables the successful deployment of CNNs on CPU-based systems, achieving substantial speedup factors, exceeding 30 times in certain cases. Our research also includes a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between parameter reduction and accuracy loss, as well as the efficiency of pruning and quantization. We provide a thorough comparison of our pruning strategy with other existing methods, highlighting its advantages and limitations. Our results show that our pruning approach outperforms other existing pruning strategies in terms of compression ratios and accuracy for a given network. This innovative approach enables the model to dynamically allocate attention to both object and non-object points within the point cloud, thereby enhancing object detection capabilities. To overcome the challenge of limited target language audio data, we explore the possibility of developing speech recognition systems without such data. Instead, we utilize text-to-speech synthesis to create a large set of artificially generated speech samples. These samples are used in conjunction with a time-delayed connection to a source language to facilitate the training of a cross-lingual encoder-decoder model. This approach allows for the adaptation of source language models, which have been successfully applied in their native context, to target languages with limited available audio. As demonstrated through our experiments, we can achieve significant word error rate reductions, specifically 29% and 1.6% relative improvements, when adapting models from English to Spanish and Portuguese, respectively. These adaptations rely on text-to-speech synthesized data and a small amount of target language audio. Moreover, we observe that our cross-lingual model exhibits improved performance in unseen domains compared to traditional fine-tuning methods. Additionally, we examine the impact of various adaptations, including prosodic variations, and find that they have a minimal effect on the overall performance of the models. These findings suggest that our approach can be a valuable tool for developing speech recognition systems in low-resource contexts. All relevant code and data are publicly available. To facilitate further research, we release our implementation on the following repository: https://github.com/NeuSRRC/XL-TTS. This repository includes the code for generating text-to-speech synthesized data, adapting models, and running the experiments described in the paper. It also includes the source code for the models themselves. It is designed to be easily extensible, allowing researchers to adapt the code to their own languages and datasets. This study delves into how party campaigns utilize voter networks by analyzing voter interaction data from a Swiss public television broadcaster with a political twist. By employing network analysis methods, the research identifies key characteristics of individual voters and the networks they form based on similar interests. This paper introduces a new forecasting model called Temporal Attention-Augmented Bilinear Network (TAABNet), designed to predict Limit Order Book (LOB) time-series data by leveraging the full LOB structure. The proposed model significantly outperforms existing methods when predicting the number of asks and bids in the next LOB snapshot. TAABNet achieves this improvement by combining LOB-level attention and bilinear network features to capture temporal LOB changes and model high-order interactions between multiple LOB elements. The model's effectiveness was validated through experiments on historical data from the NASDAQ stock market, demonstrating its superiority over other forecasting methods. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that TAABNet exhibits improved performance in long-term forecasting scenarios. The paper also provides an in-depth examination of the model's performance characteristics and potential applications. Lastly, we discuss the potential for future research in LOB time-series data forecasting. The code and model used in this study are publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/TAABNet/TAABNet. In the context of Federated Learning (FL), a significant challenge arises when training a model for multiple clients with diverse data sources, as each client's contribution to the overall loss is typically evaluated individually, leading to a prohibitively high communication cost. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative approach called pFedHN, a FedProx-like method that leverages a kernel-based approximation of the data similarity matrix, enabling more efficient use of communication resources. By employing a kernel-based approximation, we significantly reduce the complexity of the data similarity matrix, allowing for faster computation and transmission of the matrix vector product during the training process. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach through experimental results on MNIST, SVHN, and Fashion MNIST datasets. Furthermore, we show that pFedHN offers a practical solution to the communication complexity problem in FL. The code for pFedHN is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashish-behanwal/PFedHN. In multilingual BERT, fine-tuning involves adjusting both the shared multilingual encoder and the task-specific language-agnostic predictor. This study investigates how fine-tuning impacts the shared multilingual encoder and task performance. Our findings reveal that the decoder is primarily trained using task-specific training data, and its performance improves significantly during fine-tuning. Conversely, the encoder is initially trained using task-specific language-agnostic data, and its impact on task performance is initially limited. However, as the amount of task-specific training data increases, the encoder's influence on the decoder grows, leading to improved task performance. This discovery suggests that the encoder and decoder should be fine-tuned differently, and we propose a method called Multilingual Differentiated Fine-Tuning (MDFT) that adjusts the level of fine-tuning for each component based on the amount of available task-specific training data. This method outperforms Multilingual Language-agnostic Data Augmentation (mLDA) by a margin of 1.6% to 3.1% on the GLUE dataset across multiple languages. The proposed approach is further validated through ablation studies and analysis of the model's behavior. Our findings also indicate that the proposed approach is effective in handling low-resource tasks. The code and models for this research will be made publicly available. Image segmentation using hyper-Laplacian operators poses a challenge due to their non-convex nature. To address this issue, a new convex relaxation of hyper-Laplacian is introduced, enabling the application of convex optimization techniques. A corresponding dual problem is formulated and shown to be analogous to Gaussian Beltrami transport, allowing for effective initialization through statistical coupling. The proposed convex segmentation method is evaluated using both synthetic and real-world images, and compared to a non-convex tensor anisotropic diffusion algorithm. The experimental results demonstrate the advantages of the convex relaxation in image segmentation, including faster computation and robustness to noise. Additionally, the statistical coupling method is utilized to initialize the non-convex transport process, yielding superior outcomes in segmentation compared to traditional methods. In particular, the statistical coupling method is shown to produce more accurate and robust results in image segmentation, especially in complex scenarios. The proposed techniques are thoroughly evaluated through a series of experiments on multiple image datasets. The accompanying code is made available for further research and implementation.

We demonstrate that constant mean curvature surfaces in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ are one-dimensional submanifolds in the space of Gau{\ss} maps from $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ if their Gau{\ss} map is vertically harmonic. Furthermore, this classification holds under a weak assumption that the surface's third fundamental form is non-degenerate. Additionally, we categorize one-dimensional subgroups of isometric identities for constant mean curvature surfaces in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ of codimension one, providing an alternative approach to classify such surfaces. This classification is achieved by identifying the isometric group of surfaces in $\mathbb{H}^{n+1}$ of codimension one, which are modelled on the upper half-space. Our findings also reveal that the isometric group of a surface modelled on the upper half-space is modelled on the hyperbolic cylinder. Finally, we show that the isometric group of a surface modelled on the hyperbolic cylinder is categorically classified as a one-dimensional Lie group. This research is supported by the second author's Ph.D. thesis. The study also includes an appendix that outlines the formal structure of the isometric group of surfaces in $\mathbb{H}^{n+1}$ of codimension one, which are modelled on the upper half-space. Nevertheless, existing reinforcement learning methods primarily focus on user-item interaction sequences, which can overlook the time dimension and lead to biased user and item representations. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits enhanced stability and faster convergence during the recommendation process. Building on this foundation, we expand their work by introducing an additional condition for determining Wilf-equivalence in cases where the initial outcome was negative. This new criterion allows us to resolve several previously unresolved patterns listed in Table 1 of Holroyd et al's 2013 paper. Specifically, we focus on the situations where the initial patterns were non-monotone, quadratically growing, and of limited length. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive catalog of patterns along with the criteria for Wilf-equivalence. This combined effort provides a definitive understanding of the problem, superseding the partial results presented in the original paper. Additionally, we address the related open question regarding the classification of quadratically growing patterns in normal form as either Wilf-equivalent or non-equivalent. This question was first posed by Martin and Zelevinsky in 2009. By employing a novel approach involving a random coloring of the grid and the use of the cycle matroid, we are able to resolve this question in the affirmative, proving that all such patterns are indeed Wilf-equivalent. This proof relies on the use of the cycle matroid, a combinatorial object that has not previously been utilized in similar contexts. This work marks the culmination of our research into the problem initially posed by Holroyd, Martin, and Watson. The argument relies on the interplay of real multiplication, measure function, and endomorphisms, along with the non-optimal primes to derive the non-existence of smooth plane models for these curves, while also yielding new instances of optimal cases for certain curves of level 17. research, the source code used in this study has been made available on GitHub.

In experiments, IBIS-CNN significantly outperforms the current best methods, providing more accurate heart rate estimates. A cloud data center network consists of multiple servers, each containing virtual machines with diverse applications. These applications require network connections, which can be achieved through virtual networks. To optimize network resource usage, the placement of virtual networks within the physical network is a significant challenge. Research has addressed this issue, but most methods have focused on scenarios without resource failures, ignoring the need to adapt to failures in the physical network. This research proposes a failure-aware semi-centralized virtual network embedding (FSC-VNE) algorithm, which addresses the placement challenge in cloud data centers with resource failures. FSC-VNE initially creates a placement plan for virtual networks in a centralized manner, considering the failure-prone edges in the physical network. It then uses a semi-centralized approach to adjust the placement of virtual networks in response to failures, aiming to minimize the disruption and delay of networks. FSC-VNE utilizes a failure-aware virtual network embedding (FVNE) algorithm, which considers the placement history of virtual networks. To evaluate FSC-VNE's effectiveness, the algorithm is compared with existing methods in a simulated cloud data center network with resource failures. The results show that FSC-VNE significantly reduces the disruption and delay of networks caused by failures, outperforming existing methods. The algorithm also demonstrates efficiency in terms of time complexity and performance. Specifically, FSC-VNE reduces the disruption of networks by 15% and delays by 10% compared to existing methods, according to the simulation results. The algorithm also meets the time complexity requirements. The proposed FSC-VNE algorithm, combined with FVNE, provides a practical solution for resource failure handling in cloud data centers. The implementation details of FSC-VNE are provided, and the source code is available for review and evaluation. The research contributes to the development of a practical failure-aware VNE placement algorithm, which addresses the challenge of resource failure in cloud data centers. The proposed approach is expected to improve the availability and reliability of cloud data center networks. The findings also suggest that the probing time interval has a significant impact on system performance and that a time interval of 10-15 minutes yields optimal results. Ultimately, the proposed workload probing method emerges as a viable strategy for load balancing in systems with non-Poisson arrivals. The CORSIKA 8 framework is a cutting-edge tool for simulating the cascades of cosmic ray air showers and their resulting radio emissions. By utilizing a modular design, it allows users to select specific components to analyze different aspects of cosmic ray research. This study showcases the capabilities of the radio emission component, known as CORe, which can be integrated with other components to study cosmic ray physics via radio signals. CORe simulates the generation of radio waves by taking into account the spatial and temporal characteristics of particle production. Two test scenarios are presented, one examining the radio frequency behavior of a single hadronic interaction and the other exploring the effects of a cosmic ray air shower on radio emissions. The results of these simulations are compared to existing data and findings from other air shower codes, highlighting the potential of the CORSIKA 8 framework in advancing cosmic ray research. Two future research directions are also suggested. This approach enables us to demonstrate that the renormalized system exhibits non-trivial algebraic properties, including the existence of periodic points and cyclic permutations, under suitable preparation maps. Moreover, we show that the system is expansive, possesses topological mixing, and is semi-simple. We also prove the existence of a vast array of unique periodic orbits in the system. Finally, we utilize the algebraic properties of the system to construct a renormalized system for a specific class of maps defined on a compact metric space. This work is an extension of the authors' previous research, which was presented in a paper on the arXiv. A key aspect of the current paper is that it provides a novel proof of the renormalized system, which is more accessible to readers without a specialized background in dynamics. The paper also includes a comprehensive appendix that outlines the necessary background in dynamics and smooth ergodic theory required for the authors' previous research. Additionally, we provide a new proof of the semi-conjugacy theorem, which is a crucial result in the field. The paper concludes with a new perspective on the relationship between the renormalized system and the semi-invariant measure, which is a topic of ongoing research. This study examines the solvability and convergence of a generalized implicit perturbation method for variational inequality problems under relaxed solution criteria. The analysis demonstrates strong convergence towards a unique solution, with error bound estimates for the method. The paper also applies its findings to prove the existence and uniqueness of a solution to parabolic variational problems in three-dimensional space, using an iterative projected approach. These results are then utilized to analyze the dynamics of a distributed-order fractional delay differential equation, with new existence and uniqueness theorems developed through a fixed-point iteration method in a Banach space context. The paper concludes with numerical simulations verifying its results. Ultimately, it contributes to a broader understanding of variational inequality theory and its practical applications. Novel approaches are introduced for solving parabolic and fractional differential problems, with potential extensions to other non-linear problems. The study's findings can be applied to real-world engineering contexts, with specific examples in electrical and mechanical engineering, and the full paper is accessible online. \footnote{This paper is an extended version of our previously published paper in ABVM.}

Additionally, this paper provides insights into TSRL's strengths and limitations, highlighting potential avenues for improvement. We examine the relationship between covering arrays and the performance of linearly independent sets. Our analysis yields upper bounds on covering array numbers, along with a novel formula that generalizes these bounds for specific scenarios. We also establish connections between covering arrays and linearly independent sets in the context of polynomial ideals. Our findings are illustrated through examples that demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed formulas. Furthermore, we provide a logarithmic upper bound on covering array numbers, observing that such numbers grow at a rate proportional to v*t for fixed values of v and t. This is accompanied by a linear upper bound on CA(t,v,n), which holds true for all n. Recent advancements in vision-guided manipulation have primarily focused on developing end-to-end policies that connect visual input directly to robot control signals. However, these approaches often struggle with robustness to real-world conditions, including variations in lighting and object appearances. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed using a two-stage pipeline that incorporates image understanding and a separate robot control module. Nevertheless, this approach can be time-consuming and may require extensive training to generate accurate semantic maps. To address these challenges, we suggest a novel framework that combines a transformer-based model for image understanding with a separate language model that encodes robot control actions. By leveraging the strengths of both models, we can learn a direct mapping between visual input and robot control actions without sacrificing efficiency. Our proposed framework, called Prompt, enables the use of natural language prompts to guide robot control, thereby facilitating more robust and efficient task execution. Experimental results on a simulated robotic arm demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency and robustness. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical application of our framework in a real-world setting by integrating it with a mobile robot equipped with a 3D camera and a manipulator arm. In software maintenance, developers often need to look through multiple links 
between artifacts, which are usually sorted in descending order of relevance.
Traditional information retrieval models have been used to rank these links, but 
they do not consider the actual relationships between artifacts and the context 
in which links are presented. To address this issue, we developed T-BERT, a system 
that learns to rank links based on the relationships between artifacts and the context 
in which links are presented. T-BERT uses the BERT language model to extract the 
contextual relationships between artifacts, and it improves its performance by 
combining the relationships with traditional retrieval models. Our experiments show 
that T-BERT significantly outperforms traditional retrieval models and it also 
improves when the quality of links is poor. Our analysis also shows that T-BERT is 
more robust to changes in the quality of links than traditional retrieval models.

Measuring similarity between neural network architectures is a critical aspect of various research studies.  Currently available methods for comparing neural network architectures are computationally intensive, requiring the calculation of large matrices that represent pairwise relationships.  These approaches are often impractical due to their high computational demands.  We present a new method for normalizing and scaling neural network parameters, which enables more efficient comparison of neural network architectures.  Using this approach, we can calculate the relationships between any two sets of neural network parameters in a matter of seconds, significantly reducing the time required for comparison.  These improvements are made possible by leveraging the properties of dot product space, where the calculation of distances between vectors is facilitated through the use of matrix multiplication.  As a result, we can efficiently compare neural network architectures with varying numbers of parameters.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a large collection of neural network models, and show that it yields meaningful and interpretable results.  Specifically, we find that our scaling method is effective in identifying related architectures and distinguishing between different neural network types.  These findings are consistent with the results obtained using other comparison methods, underscoring the robustness of our approach.  Additionally, we highlight the potential of this method for analyzing neural network architectures in relation to their performance on specific tasks.  As such, we believe that this approach has the potential to facilitate a deeper understanding of neural network behavior. In this study, we propose a versatile pricing framework that adapts to various auction types, incorporating a dynamic reserve price system. This framework is tailored for the online advertising market where publishers can utilize multiple ad exchanges with different auction mechanisms. Our framework's core benefit lies in striking a balance between maximizing revenue generation and minimizing the long-term degradation of user experience, which is contingent upon the display of high-priced ads. Notably, we demonstrate that achieving both revenue maximization and preserving user experience is possible within a Bayesian game setting, where publishers act as players in a repeated game. Our model's performance is demonstrated through a simulation based on real-world data from a major publisher, showcasing significant revenue gains and minimal adverse impacts on user experience. Furthermore, we examine the impact of auction type on our framework's performance and present a practical approach to implementing the proposed system. Knowledge distillation, where a simpler model (student) is trained by a more complex model (teacher), has emerged as a prominent approach.  However, selecting the ideal teacher model is crucial for knowledge distillation's success.  Typically, the teacher model is either a fully converged model or an intermediate model that was not fully converged during training.  In this study, we investigate whether intermediate models can serve as effective teachers by outperforming both intermediate and converged teacher models.  To this end, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the learning dynamics of neural networks and discovered that intermediate models possess valuable knowledge that can be leveraged for better learning outcomes.  Experimental results demonstrate that intermediate models can indeed outperform both intermediate and converged teacher models, yielding a more efficient and effective knowledge distillation method.  Furthermore, we propose a novel method for selecting the optimal intermediate teacher model based on its knowledge capacity, which can be measured by tracking the gradients of the intermediate neurons during training.  This new approach is straightforward to implement and can be applied to a wide range of neural networks.  Experiment results confirm that intermediate teacher models can outperform fully converged teacher models and achieve superior knowledge distillation outcomes.  Additionally, we demonstrate that intermediate teacher models can be more efficient than their fully converged counterparts, reducing the training time of the student model. Depth estimation from a single image is a challenging yet significant computer vision task, with numerous applications. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to improved performance in this field. This paper introduces a novel depth prediction method, center-aware depth encoding (CDE), that transforms the task into a classification problem. By doing so, CDE achieves a more accurate and efficient solution compared to traditional regression-based approaches. To this end, CDE employs a multi-scale convolutional architecture to capture local and global features, followed by a center-aware module that extracts the essential semantic information. This is achieved by identifying the center pixel and aggregating features from neighboring areas. Finally, CDE fuses the outputs of its center-aware module and a classification head through a center-aware decoder to produce a depth map. Experimental results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that CDE significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and model efficiency. Notably, CDE achieves a 1.5% improvement in NMSE and 1.8% improvement in MAE on the DTU dataset, while reducing the model size by 2.5 times and inference time by 3.5 times. We introduce a quantum decision problem, modelled within the quantum automata framework, specifically on quantum finite state machines with one bit of memory and one bit of workspace. This problem, $k$-sum, requires determining whether the largest odd divisor of a given positive integer $k$ is equal to $k$ itself. Notably, $k$-sum is proven to be computationally intractable for quantum finite state machines with one bit of memory and one bit of workspace. Furthermore, $k$-sum is also demonstrated to be computationally intractable for quantum finite state machines with one bit of workspace and a restricted quantum gate set that includes only the Hadamard gate and the CNOT gate. In a diverse social network where connections facilitate differing viewpoints, 
the interplay between link formation dynamics and individual interactions 
determines the level of polarization among group members. This study 
investigates the polarization levels that arise in networks where users can 
interact with one another after establishing connections, and where connections 
are established with users who share similar interests or who have similar 
views. We examine two distinct scenarios: one where users are randomly connected 
and another where users are connected in a structured manner. Our results reveal 
that higher polarization is associated with increased diversity of user opinions 
and enhanced link formation between users with similar interests or views. 
Furthermore, we found that structured networks tend to polarize more rapidly than 
completely random networks. These findings have significant implications for the 
design of social media platforms aimed at mitigating polarization among users. 
Our study provides valuable insights into the relationship between social network 
structure and user interactions, and highlights the importance of understanding 
polarization in modern social media platforms. These findings can inform the 
development of effective strategies to reduce polarization among users. 
The study's results are also applicable to other areas, such as political campaigns, 
where understanding polarization dynamics can inform strategies to achieve 
social cohesion. By examining the interplay between social network structure and 
user interactions, we can develop a deeper understanding of polarization and 
pave the way for the development of effective strategies to reduce polarization. 
The findings of this study can also be extended to other domains where social 
interactions and network dynamics are at play.

freely.

A key component of first-order and second-order algorithms for optimizing complex problems is the computation of gradients and Hessians. However, many such algorithms have been developed for a specific type of optimization problem, known as a composite problem. In this paper, we establish a fundamental link between a more general framework, called a lower-level problem, and a composite problem. This link is based on a mathematical theorem, the implicit function theorem (IFT), which allows us to derive a useful formula for computing gradients and Hessians. These models are well-suited to handle correlations and structural changes, making them ideal for analyzing long datasets with significant breaks. However, existing models are limited by the assumption that break points align with the analysis interval, necessitating the development of new methods that can account for this discrepancy. In response, we introduce a novel estimation approach that leverages a penalized sum-of-squares objective function to estimate the break points and transition parameters. We demonstrate that this method can be used in a multi-stage process to estimate key parameters, and provide conditions for consistent estimation of break points and transition functions. Furthermore, we derive asymptotic properties of the transition function estimators and provide numerical examples that illustrate the performance of our approach. We also apply our method to real-world data, specifically the global temperature anomaly series, to estimate its piecewise stationary parameters. The results show that our method can lead to a more accurate understanding of climate change, and provide insights into the global temperature anomaly series. The results indicate that our method can be used for robust segmentation of time series data, and provide insights into the global temperature anomaly series. We investigate the impact of delayed optical feedback on the pulsing behavior of microlasers in and out of the linear regime, utilizing a microscopic model based on the Maxwell-Bloch equations. These equations are solved through a variational approach, with the resulting approximate solutions being compared to the exact solutions obtained through a numerical scheme. By analyzing the relationship between delay and detuning, we identify the conditions necessary for the emergence of periodic and chaotic attractors in the laser's time-domain dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the laser's time-domain behavior influences its spectral characteristics, with delayed optical feedback resulting in distinct changes to the laser's spectrum. The findings of this study are validated through numerical simulations and experiments conducted on a semiconductor microlaser. Additionally, we explore the potential applications of microlasers with delayed optical feedback in quantum state transfer and entangled particle generation. The results of this research provide valuable insights into the dynamics of microlasers and their potential uses in quantum communication technology. Finally, we discuss the relevance of our findings to the study of ultrafast photonics.
